content.title: Define a specific target segment and size it
content.finding: No specific target segment has been defined, and no method has been used to size the market — the business's understanding of who it sells to and how large that opportunity is rests on assumption rather than definition.
content.consequence: Without a defined segment, decisions about product, pricing, and where to spend effort finding customers are all being made without a clear target to aim at — everything downstream is guessing at who it's for.
content.action: Define a specific target segment — who exactly the business sells to — and produce one sizing estimate for it, even a simple one, so there's a stated number rather than an impression.
content.avoid: Describing the target market so broadly ("everyone who needs X") that it doesn't actually narrow anything. A segment that includes almost anyone isn't a defined segment.
content.action_evidence: A specific target segment is written down, along with a single sizing estimate.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: is the target segment loosely defined, with a sizing estimate, even without a stated method? A "yes" answer (B) resolves this item.

content.title: Sharpen the segment definition and add a stated sizing method
content.finding: The target segment is loosely defined, and the market sizing is a single estimate with no stated method behind it — there's a number, but not yet a reason to trust it.
content.consequence: Decisions resting on this sizing estimate — how big an opportunity to chase, how much to invest — are resting on a number that can't currently be defended or checked.
content.action: Sharpen the target segment definition to be specific rather than loose, and produce the sizing estimate using one stated method (bottom-up from unit economics, or top-down from a broader market figure), with assumptions written down.
content.avoid: Adding a bigger, more impressive-sounding total addressable market figure without changing the method behind it. A larger unsupported number is not more rigorous than a smaller one.
content.action_evidence: The target segment is specifically defined, and the sizing estimate has one documented method with stated assumptions.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: is the segment clearly and specifically defined, with sizing using one stated method and documented assumptions? A "yes" answer (C) resolves this item.

content.title: Back the sizing estimate with credible external sources
content.finding: The target segment is clearly and specifically defined, and sizing uses one stated method with assumptions — solid, but the sizing still rests entirely on the business's own assumptions rather than any external source.
content.consequence: The sizing estimate is only as credible as the assumptions behind it, and right now nothing outside the business's own reasoning backs those assumptions up.
content.action: Bring in credible external sources — industry data, published research, comparable company figures — to support the sizing assumptions, and document where each one comes from.
content.avoid: Citing a single, unverified secondary source (a blog post, a vendor's marketing claim) as if it were rigorous external validation.
content.action_evidence: The sizing estimate cites specific, credible external sources for its key assumptions, documented alongside them.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: does sizing use credible external sources with assumptions documented? A "yes" answer (D) resolves this item.

content.title: Have the first real conversations with potential customers
content.finding: There has been no direct contact with potential customers — belief that customers will choose and pay for this specific solution currently rests on assumption rather than any conversation with the people who would actually buy it.
content.consequence: Every decision built on top of this assumption — what to build, how to position it, who to target — is currently unverified. If the underlying belief about demand is wrong, everything built on it needs to be redone.
content.action: Have informal conversations with a handful of potential customers representative of the target segment, specifically about the problem this offering addresses — not a pitch, a conversation about whether the problem is real and how they currently deal with it.
content.avoid: Talking only to friends, family, or people predisposed to be supportive. Their interest doesn't tell you what a genuine prospect would say.
content.action_evidence: A handful of informal conversations with potential customers have taken place and show real interest in the problem.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: do informal conversations show interest, even if cost or urgency of the problem is unconfirmed? A "yes" answer (B) resolves this item.

content.title: Confirm the problem is real and worth solving, not just interesting
content.finding: Informal conversations show interest, but whether the problem is costly or urgent enough to act on remains unconfirmed.
content.consequence: Interest alone doesn't distinguish a real, worth-solving problem from a mild annoyance customers would never actually pay to fix — the business doesn't yet know which one it has.
content.action: Hold documented conversations with customers representative of the target segment, specifically probing whether the problem is real and worth solving — not just interesting to discuss.
content.avoid: Counting polite agreement ("yeah, that would be nice") as confirmation the problem is worth solving. Look for evidence they've already tried to solve it themselves, or would pay to.
content.action_evidence: Documented conversations with representative customers confirm the problem is real and worth solving.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: do documented conversations confirm the problem is real and worth solving, even if willingness to pay is untested? A "yes" answer (C) resolves this item.

content.title: Get specific purchase intent, not just confirmed interest
content.finding: Documented conversations confirm the problem is real and worth solving, but willingness to pay for this specific solution remains untested.
content.consequence: The business knows the problem matters to customers, but not yet whether they'll choose to pay this business, specifically, to solve it — the gap between "this problem matters" and "I'll pay you for this" is where many otherwise-promising ideas stall.
content.action: Get representative customers to express specific purchase intent — a letter of intent, a pilot agreement, or a deposit — even without collecting full revenue yet.
content.avoid: Treating enthusiastic verbal commitment ("I'd definitely buy this") as purchase intent. Only something the customer would have to act on — a signature, a deposit — counts.
content.action_evidence: At least one representative customer has signed a letter of intent, pilot agreement, or paid a deposit.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: have representative customers expressed specific purchase intent, even without revenue collected? A "yes" answer (D) resolves this item.

content.title: Articulate a reason customers would choose this business
content.finding: There is no articulated reason for a customer to choose this business over alternatives, including doing nothing.
content.consequence: Without a stated reason to choose this business, every sale currently depends on the prospect arriving at that reason on their own — an unreliable and unrepeatable basis for winning business.
content.action: Articulate a specific reason customers would choose this business over alternatives (including doing nothing), even if it isn't yet a strong or defensible one.
content.avoid: Reaching for a generic claim ("we care more," "better service") that could describe almost any competitor. The reason needs to be specific to this business.
content.action_evidence: A specific reason for choosing this business is written down and used consistently in customer conversations.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: does a reason exist, even if weak or easily matched? A "yes" answer (B) resolves this item.

content.title: Get the differentiator confirmed by customers, not just asserted
content.finding: A reason to choose this business exists but is weak or easily matched, and isn't supported by research or customer input.
content.consequence: The current reason to choose this business over alternatives probably wouldn't survive a determined competitor testing it — it's an assertion, not something customers have confirmed matters to them.
content.action: Test the stated reason with real customer input or research — confirm it's something customers actually value and would choose the business for, not just something the business believes distinguishes it.
content.avoid: Assuming the reason is valid because it sounds convincing internally. Internal conviction isn't customer confirmation.
content.action_evidence: Customer research or direct customer confirmation supports the stated differentiator as something that actually matters to them.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: does a meaningful, customer-supported difference exist, even if realistically copyable? A "yes" answer (C) resolves this item.

content.title: Make the differentiator structurally hard to copy
content.finding: A meaningful, customer-confirmed difference exists, but it's realistically copyable by a competitor — nothing currently protects it.
content.consequence: Whatever advantage the business currently holds is borrowed time — a competitor with the will to copy it could close the gap, and nothing structural stops them.
content.action: Build a structural defensibility factor around the existing differentiator — a switching cost, proprietary process or data, exclusive access, brand trust, network effect, or cost advantage — so the difference becomes harder to copy.
content.avoid: Trying to out-market the difference (louder claims, more visibility) instead of making it structurally harder to replicate. Visibility doesn't create defensibility.
content.action_evidence: A specific structural defensibility factor is identifiably in place around the existing differentiator.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: is the meaningful difference now backed by a structural defensibility factor? A "yes" answer (D) resolves this item.

content.title: Start tracking market conditions
content.finding: There is no awareness of market conditions and no deliberate response to them — the business operates purely reactively to whatever the market does.
content.consequence: Changes in the market — shifting demand, new competitors, changing customer needs — currently arrive as surprises rather than things the business saw coming and could plan for.
content.action: Start deliberately tracking the market conditions that matter to this business — demand direction, competitive moves, customer shifts — even informally, so a general impression starts to form.
content.avoid: Confusing occasional anecdotes ("I heard a competitor is struggling") with actual tracking. A general impression needs to come from consistently paying attention, not isolated data points.
content.action_evidence: The business can describe a general, current impression of its market conditions, formed through ongoing attention rather than a one-off observation.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: does a general impression of market conditions exist, even without a deliberate response yet? A "yes" answer (B) resolves this item.

content.title: Ground the market read and put together a response plan
content.finding: A general impression of market conditions exists, but no deliberate response is in motion.
content.consequence: The business is aware something is happening in its market but isn't yet acting on that awareness — the value of noticing a shift is lost if nothing is done in response to it.
content.action: Understand market conditions with more rigor — sourced information, not impression — and put together a response plan, even if it isn't fully executed yet.
content.avoid: Building an elaborate response plan without first grounding the market read in sourced information. A well-organized response to a wrong read doesn't help.
content.action_evidence: A sourced understanding of market conditions exists, along with a written response plan.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: is there a sourced understanding of conditions and a response plan, even if not fully executed? A "yes" answer (C) resolves this item.

content.title: Execute the response strategy, not just plan it
content.finding: Market conditions are understood with rigor and a response plan exists, but it isn't yet being fully executed.
content.consequence: The business knows what it should be doing about its market conditions but hasn't yet closed the gap between planning and doing — the conditions the plan was built to address keep moving in the meantime.
content.action: Actively execute the response strategy already planned, rather than leaving it as an unexecuted plan.
content.avoid: Repeatedly revising the plan instead of executing the current version. A plan that's always being refined and never acted on doesn't move this item.
content.action_evidence: The response strategy is visibly being executed — specific actions from the plan have actually been taken.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: is a deliberate strategy suited to market conditions being actively executed? A "yes" answer (D) resolves this item.

content.title: Try or plan a specific acquisition method
content.finding: There is no identifiable method for reaching new customers — customers arrive coincidentally, or not at all.
content.consequence: Without any repeatable way of reaching customers, growth currently depends on chance rather than anything the business can plan around or scale.
content.action: Try or plan a specific method for reaching the target segment — a channel, an outreach approach, a partnership — even if it hasn't yet proven it can reliably reach them.
content.avoid: Trying several channels briefly and superficially instead of committing to testing one long enough to know if it works.
content.action_evidence: A specific method for reaching customers has been tried or planned, even without proven reliability yet.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: has a method been tried or planned, even without proven reliability? A "yes" answer (B) resolves this item.

content.title: Prove the channel reliably reaches and engages the target segment
content.finding: A method for reaching customers has been tried or planned, but it hasn't shown it can reliably reach the target segment.
content.consequence: The business doesn't yet know if its acquisition approach actually works — effort is being spent on a channel whose reliability is still unproven.
content.action: Keep using the channel until it reliably reaches and engages the target segment — even before converting them — so its reliability is demonstrated, not assumed.
content.avoid: Switching channels every time results are slow, rather than giving one channel enough sustained effort to actually know if it works.
content.action_evidence: The channel is reliably reaching and engaging the target segment, even if not yet converting them to paying customers or active users.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: does a specific channel reliably reach and engage the target segment, even before conversion? A "yes" answer (C) resolves this item.

content.title: Convert engagement into active users or pilot participants
content.finding: A channel reliably reaches and engages the target segment, but it hasn't yet repeatedly converted them into active users or pilot participants.
content.consequence: Reaching and engaging people is necessary but not sufficient — until engagement turns into real participation, the business doesn't know if the channel actually produces anything more than attention.
content.action: Focus the channel specifically on converting engaged prospects into active users or pilot participants, and be able to explain why the channel works — what about it makes conversion happen.
content.avoid: Counting a growing list of engaged followers or subscribers as progress, without converting any meaningful share of them into actual users or pilots.
content.action_evidence: The channel has repeatedly converted reached prospects into active users or pilot participants, with a clear explanation of why it works.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: does the channel repeatedly convert reached prospects into active users or pilot participants, with an explanation of why? A "yes" answer (D) resolves this item.

content.title: Convert engagement into paying customers
content.finding: A channel reliably reaches and engages the target segment, but it hasn't yet repeatedly converted them into paying customers.
content.consequence: Reaching and engaging prospects is necessary but not sufficient — until engagement turns into paying customers, the channel isn't yet proven as a real acquisition mechanism.
content.action: Focus the channel specifically on converting engaged prospects into paying customers, and be able to explain why the channel works — what about it makes conversion happen.
content.avoid: Treating a high volume of engagement (clicks, inquiries, leads) as success without tracking how much of it actually converts to paying customers.
content.action_evidence: The channel has repeatedly converted reached prospects into paying customers, with a clear explanation of why it works.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: does the channel repeatedly convert reached prospects into paying customers, with an explanation of why? A "yes" answer (D) resolves this item.

content.title: Look for the first signs of continued relationship
content.finding: There is no evidence that customers stay engaged, return, or advocate for the business over time.
content.consequence: The business doesn't yet know whether it earns repeat relationships or has to win every customer fresh each time — a much more expensive and fragile way to grow.
content.action: Look for and note any positive signals of continued relationship — a customer who came back, referred someone, or gave unprompted positive feedback — even isolated ones.
content.avoid: Assuming satisfaction because no one has complained. Absence of complaints isn't evidence of continued relationship.
content.action_evidence: At least one isolated positive signal of continued relationship or advocacy has been identified and noted.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: are there isolated positive signals, even without a pattern across customers? A "yes" answer (B) resolves this item.

content.title: Find the pattern across customers, not just the standouts
content.finding: Isolated positive signals of continued relationship exist, but no pattern has emerged across customers.
content.consequence: The business can't yet tell whether a good relationship is typical or a lucky exception — without a pattern, there's no basis for expecting it to repeat.
content.action: Look across multiple customers, not just the ones that stand out, for whatever pattern of continued relationship is natural to this business — repeat purchase, renewal, extension, follow-on work, or unprompted positive feedback.
content.avoid: Cherry-picking the best few customer relationships as if they represented the norm, rather than looking honestly across the base.
content.action_evidence: A pattern of continued relationship is identifiable across multiple customers, even if not yet formally tracked.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: does a pattern of continued relationship exist across multiple customers, even if untracked? A "yes" answer (C) resolves this item.

content.title: Start tracking the retention pattern consistently
content.finding: A pattern of continued relationship exists across multiple customers, but it isn't consistently tracked.
content.consequence: Without tracking, the business can't tell if this pattern is improving, declining, or stable — it's relying on a general sense rather than a measured one.
content.action: Start consistently tracking the identified pattern across the customers relevant to the business's natural engagement cycle, so it becomes a measured fact rather than an impression.
content.avoid: Tracking the pattern for a single period and treating that as sufficient. Consistency means an ongoing practice, not a one-time count.
content.action_evidence: The pattern of continued relationship is being tracked consistently across the relevant customer base.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: is that pattern consistently tracked across the customers relevant to the business's natural engagement cycle? A "yes" answer (D) resolves this item.

content.title: Follow up and see who stays engaged informally
content.finding: No one who has engaged with the concept has stayed engaged, or been willing to vouch for it beyond an initial conversation.
content.consequence: The business doesn't yet have any evidence that interest in the concept survives beyond a first conversation — a real risk that early interest is polite rather than genuine.
content.action: Follow up with people who showed initial interest and see whether any stay engaged informally — even a small, informal handful is a starting signal.
content.avoid: Interpreting silence after an initial conversation as continued interest. Lack of a negative response isn't evidence of engagement.
content.action_evidence: A few people who showed initial interest remain informally engaged with the concept.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: do a few isolated people remain informally engaged, even without anything sustained? A "yes" answer (B) resolves this item.

content.title: Form a defined, engaged group
content.finding: A few isolated people remain informally engaged with the concept, but nothing sustained has developed.
content.consequence: Isolated informal interest doesn't yet tell the business whether it has a real group of engaged early adopters to build from, or just a few polite well-wishers.
content.action: Form a defined group — design partners, a waitlist, pilot testers — and get them engaged across more than one touchpoint, rather than leaving engagement informal and scattered.
content.avoid: Counting a large but passive email list as a defined, engaged group. The construct requires actual engagement across touchpoints, not just a list of names.
content.action_evidence: A defined group exists and has engaged with the concept across multiple touchpoints.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: has a defined group stayed engaged across multiple touchpoints? A "yes" answer (C) resolves this item.

content.title: Get the group to re-engage on its own initiative
content.finding: A defined group has stayed engaged across multiple touchpoints, but hasn't yet proactively re-engaged on their own initiative.
content.consequence: Sustained engagement the business has to keep initiating is weaker evidence than engagement the group initiates itself — the business doesn't yet know if this group would act without being prompted.
content.action: Look for and encourage proactive re-engagement from the group — extending a pilot, referring someone else, agreeing to a reference call — rather than the business always being the one to reach out.
content.avoid: Prompting a reference call or referral so directly that it's effectively the business's initiative rather than the group's. The point is the group acting on its own.
content.action_evidence: At least one member of the group has proactively re-engaged — extended a pilot, made a referral, or agreed to a reference call — without being asked.
content.assessment_evidence: Re-asked: has the group proactively re-engaged in one of these ways? A "yes" answer (D) resolves this item.
